exampleAnswers.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Using the Product Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms share the same base, and so we can combine them using the product rule, as follows:

\begin{align*} 4\log \left( 5 \right) + 4\log \left( x \right) &= 8\\[5pt] 4\left[ {\log \left( 5 \right) + \log \left( x \right)} \right] &= 8\\[5pt] 4 \log \left( {5x} \right) &= 8\\[5pt] \log \left( {5x} \right) &= \dfrac{8}{4}\\[5pt] \log \left( {5x} \right) &= 2 \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} {10^{\log \left( {5x} \right)}} &= {10^2}\\[5pt] 5x &= {100}\\[5pt] x &= 20 \end{align*}

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Using the Product Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms share the same base, and so we can combine them using the product rule, as follows:

\begin{align*} \ln(8) + \ln(x-1) &= 0 \\[5pt] \ln \left(8(x-1)\right) &= 0 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} e^{\ln \left(8(x-1)\right)} &=e^{0}\\[5pt] 8(x-1) &= 1 \\[5pt] 8x-8 &= 1\\[5pt] 8x &= 9\\[5pt] x&=\dfrac {9}{8} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Using the Quotient Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms share the same base, and so we can combine them using the quotient rule, as follows:

\begin{align*} \ln \left( x \right) - \ln \left( 2 \right) &= 1\\[5pt] \ln \left( {\dfrac{x}{2}} \right) &= 1\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} {e^{\ln \left(x/2 \right)}} &= {e^1}\\[5pt] \dfrac{x}{2} &= {e}\\[5pt] x &= 2e \end{align*}

example.title: Solving Logarithmic Equations Using the Quotient Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms share the same base, and so we can combine them using the quotient rule, as follows:

\begin{align*} \ln \left( x \right) - \ln \left( 12 \right) &= 4 \\[5pt] \ln \left( {\dfrac{x}{12}} \right) &= 4\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} e^{\ln \left( x/12\right)} &= e^4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{x}{12} &= e^4\\[5pt] x &= 12e^4 \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Solving Equations Resulting in Quadratic Equations Using the Product Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms share the same base, so we can combine them using the product rule as follows:

\begin{align*} \log_5 \left(6\right) + \log_5 \left(2x^2\right) &= \log_5 \left(48\right)\\[5pt] \log_5 \left(6\cdot 2x^2\right) &= \log_5 \left(48\right)\\[5pt] \log_5 \left(12x^2\right) &= \log_5 \left(48\right)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} 5^{\log_5 \left(12x^2\right)} &=5^{\log_5 \left(48\right)}\\[5pt] 12x^2 &= 48\\[5pt] x^2 &= 4\\[5pt] x &= \pm 2 \end{align*}

So, $x=2$ or $x=-2$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting them back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=2$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_5 \left(6\right) + \log_5 \left(2\cdot 2^2\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(6\right) + \log_5 \left(8\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(6\cdot 8\right) &\stackrel{?}{=}\log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(48\right) &= \log_5 \left(48\right). \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=2$ is a valid solution.

  • Substituting $x=-2$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_5 \left(6\right) + \log_5 \left(2(-2)^2\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(6\right) + \log_5 \left(8\right) &\stackrel{?}{=} \log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(6\cdot 8\right) &\stackrel{?}{=}\log_5 \left(48\right) \\[5pt] \log_5 \left(48\right) &= \log_5 \left(48\right). \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=-2$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=\pm 2.$"

example.title: Solving Equations Resulting in Quadratic Equations Using the Product Rule

question.explanation:
The logarithms on the left-hand side share the same base, so we can combine them using the product rule as follows:

\begin{align*} \log_{6}(x+ 3) + \log_{6}(2-x) &= 1 \\[5pt] \log_{6}\left[(x + 3)(2-x)\right] &= 1 \\ \end{align*}

Now, we solve the equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} (x +3)(2-x) &= 6^1 \\[5pt] 2x-x^2+6 -3x &= 6 \\[5pt] x^2+x &= 0 \\[5pt] x(x +1) &= 0. \end{align*}

So, $x = 0$ or $x = -1.$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting them back into the original equation:

  • Substituting $x=0$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_{6}(0 +3) + \log_{6}(2-0) &\stackrel{?}{=}1 \\[5pt] \log_{6}(3) + \log_{6}(2)&\stackrel{?}{=}1\\[5pt] \log_{6}(3\cdot 2)&\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_{6}(6)&\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 1&=1.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=0$ is a valid solution.

  • Substituting $x=-1$ back into the original equation, we get \begin{align*} \log_{6}(-1 +3) + \log_{6}(2-(-1)) &\stackrel{?}{=}1 \\[5pt] \log_{6}(2) + \log_{6}(3)&\stackrel{?}{=}1\\[5pt] \log_{6}(2\cdot 3)&\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] \log_{6}(6)&\stackrel{?}{=} 1 \\[5pt] 1&=1.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} Therefore, $x=-1$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$x=0$ and $x=-1$".
